query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (approximately 35 at% Ti, 35 at% Ni, and 10 at% each of Co, Cr, and Fe), implementing a post-sintering aging treatment at 900 °C for 4 hours will produce a uniform dispersion of nanometer-scale, ordered TiNi (B2) intermetallic precipitates within the disordered matrix, resulting in an approximately 20–30% increase in elevated-temperature (∼800 °C) yield strength and improved creep resistance relative to the same alloy processed only by spark plasma sintering without the aging treatment.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully dense, homogenized Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy with nominal composition around Ti35Ni35Co10Cr10Fe10 (all at%) produced by spark plasma sintering.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-sintering aging heat treatment at 900 °C for 4 hours followed by controlled cooling.
generation.conditions: Aging conducted in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation; evaluation of mechanical properties at elevated temperatures (∼800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of uniformly distributed, nanoscale (e.g., 10–50 nm) ordered TiNi (B2) precipitates within the disordered high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The controlled aging treatment induces a precipitation reaction; the nanoscale TiNi precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening) and impede creep deformation at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in elevated-temperature yield strength by approximately 20–30% and improved creep resistance, relative to the as-sintered alloy without the aging treatment.
generation.baseline: The same Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy produced solely by spark plasma sintering without any subsequent aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The composition must remain within the HEA limits (each element 5–35 at%), with Ti and Ni maintained as the primary constituents; aging temperature and time should be controlled (900 °C for 4 hours) to avoid overaging or formation of coarse detrimental phases; evaluation at temperatures around 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage improvement in yield strength may vary with slight deviations in composition or heat treatment parameters, and the stability of the precipitate phase at prolonged high-temperature exposure needs further confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Ti35Ni35Co10Cr10Fe10 HEA by spark plasma sintering. Subject one set to the post-sintering aging treatment at 900 °C for 4 hours under inert atmosphere and leave the other set as-sintered. Characterize the microstructure using TEM to confirm the presence or absence of nanoscale, ordered TiNi precipitates and perform elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests (at ∼800 °C) on both sets.
measurements: TEM micrographs to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Elevated-temperature yield strength and creep rate measurements using a high-temperature mechanical testing system.
Comparative analysis of hardness via microhardness testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the aged samples either do not show the formation of the targeted nanoscale ordered TiNi precipitates or if the elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance of the aged samples are not statistically significantly higher (by roughly 20–30%) than those of the as-sintered baseline samples.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti High-Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti high-entropy alloy produced via directed energy deposition (DED), with a multicomponent FCC (and possibly γ + γ′) microstructure
papers.approach: Additive manufacturing to achieve rapid solidification and a uniform microstructure; alloy design tuned by adjusting Al and Ti content to induce a dual-phase (γ + γ′) structure
papers.findings: The formation of a γ + γ′ phase within the FCC HEA matrix enhanced tensile strength, microhardness and provided better high-temperature stability, indicating potential for superior elevated-temperature mechanical properties
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening through the formation of an ordered intermetallic (γ′) phase, which resists coarsening and creep at high temperatures

papers.title: Microstructure and Properties of NiCoCrAlTi High Entropy Alloy Prepared Using MA-SPS Technique.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlTi high-entropy alloy produced via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering; composition emphasizes both nickel and titanium as major constituents
papers.approach: Powder metallurgy with MA-SPS processing to control microstructural evolution and phase formation for high-temperature applications (e.g., aero-engines)
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited promising mechanical properties and thermal stability, suggesting that when Ni and Ti are primary constituents, optimized processing can yield improved elevated-temperature performance
papers.mechanism: Solid-solution and precipitation strengthening effects due to the controlled formation of a uniform microstructure that is stable at elevated temperatures

papers.title: Influence of Titanium on Microstructure, Phase Formation and Wear Behaviour of AlCoCrFeNiTiₓ High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with varying titanium contents (x = 0.0 to 1.5); while nickel is a major constituent, titanium is varied to study its effect
papers.approach: Systematic variation of titanium content to observe microstructural evolution, including precipitation of secondary phases and dendritic structures, with implications for mechanical properties
papers.findings: With moderate titanium additions (x around 0.5), improved phase stability and wear resistance were observed; too high titanium content led to complex phase formation that may embrittle the alloy
papers.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening from titanium’s large atomic radius and its role in stabilizing secondary phases, potentially promoting a beneficial balance between ductility and strength

papers.title: Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy (Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr) containing titanium as one of several principal refractory elements
papers.approach: Investigation of refractory element additions using arc melting, with titanium playing a dual role as a beta stabilizer and solid solution strengthener
papers.findings: The inclusion of titanium influenced phase stability and solid solution strengthening; however, the alloy systems predominantly treated titanium as one of several additions rather than as a primary constituent
papers.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening via lattice distortion and beta phase stabilization provided by titanium, contributing to high elevated-temperature strength

established: HEAs with compositions between 5–35 at% per element form single-phase solid solutions or simple dual-phase mixtures with high configurational entropy.
Refractory and nickel-based HEAs can achieve high elevated-temperature strength and oxidation resistance via tailored microstructures.
Precipitation strengthening (e.g., formation of ordered γ′ phases) and solid-solution strengthening play a key role in achieving high-temperature mechanical properties.

approaches_tried.approach: Additive manufacturing (e.g., DED) to control rapid solidification and microstructural uniformity in Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti alloys.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced tensile strength and microhardness through the formation of a beneficial dual-phase (γ + γ′) structure at elevated temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Powder metallurgy (mechanical alloying coupled with spark plasma sintering) for processing NiCoCrAlTi HEAs.
approaches_tried.outcome: Obtained favorable high-temperature properties through controlled phase formation and microstructural stability.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled variation of titanium content in AlCoCrFeNi-based systems to modify microstructure and intermetallic formation.
approaches_tried.outcome: Discovery of an optimal titanium level (moderate addition) that enhances wear resistance and provides clues for improved mechanical properties; excessive titanium leads to deleterious phase complexity.

mechanisms: Precipitation strengthening through formation of ordered phases such as γ′ that hinder dislocation motion at high temperatures.
Solid-solution strengthening by incorporating elements (e.g., titanium) with larger atomic radii, leading to lattice distortions that resist deformation.
Control of dislocation behavior (edge vs. screw dislocation motion) influenced by alloy chemistry and microstructural features.
disagreements: Debate over the dominant dislocation mechanism (edge versus screw) that controls strength in high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures.
Varying findings on the effects of high titanium content; while moderate additions improve mechanical properties, excessive additions may lead to formation of brittle intermetallics.
open_questions: How do primary-element systems (with both titanium and nickel as main constituents) behave compared to traditional HEAs where titanium or nickel are secondary additions?
What is the optimum processing condition (e.g., heat treatment schedule) to precisely control the formation and stability of beneficial precipitate phases in a Ti-Ni primary HEA?
How do targeted microstructural interventions influence dislocation dynamics at elevated temperatures in such uniquely composed HEAs?
opportunities: Exploring heat treatment or rapid cooling interventions to induce a fine, uniform precipitation of ordered phases (e.g., γ′) in titanium- and nickel-primary HEAs.
Combining additive manufacturing with tailored alloy compositions that treat Ti and Ni as primary constituents to achieve dual-phase microstructures optimized for high-temperature applications.

Investigating processing–composition–microstructure relationships in new Ti-Ni dominant HEA systems to fine-tune elevated-temperature mechanical properties, with potential for coupling with refractory element adjustments.

directions.direction: Tailored post-sintering aging heat treatment to induce fine, ordered TiNi intermetallic precipitates for precipitation strengthening.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the elevated-temperature mechanical performance by creating nanoscale, ordered precipitates that impede dislocation motion. It uses well‐established precipitation strengthening physics and builds on evidence from studies showing γ + γ′ dual-phase microstructures yield improved strength (e.g., PMC11396108::web::001::abstract). The intervention respects the constraint of maintaining a high-entropy composition with Ti and Ni primary, and the process is experimentally feasible with techniques like spark plasma sintering followed by controlled aging.

directions.direction: Composition design via minor alloying additions that favor the formation of a dual-phase microstructure with ordered intermetallics.
directions.assessment: This direction involves slight modifications in the nominal composition (e.g., adding small amounts of Al or Cr) to promote an ordered phase formation. While it can leverage solid-solution and precipitation strengthening as seen in related systems (PMC7513041::web::002::1_introduction), it may face challenges in keeping all elements within the required 5–35 at% range and ensuring Ti and Ni remain the primary constituents.

directions.direction: Processing route adjustment using rapid solidification techniques (such as additive manufacturing) to refine the microstructure.
directions.assessment: Rapid solidification can limit grain growth and enhance phase control. However, while localized cooling rates can favor refined microstructures, the technique may be less specific in promoting the controlled precipitation necessary for elevated-temperature strengthening, making the causal link less direct than targeted aging.

directions.direction: Surface treatment or coating to improve oxidation resistance and indirectly enhance elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
directions.assessment: Surface coatings (e.g., oxidation-resistant layers) can protect the alloy at high temperatures and may indirectly contribute to mechanical reliability. However, this approach does not modify the bulk microstructure responsible for creep and yield strength and thus does not directly address the primary limitation in high-temperature strength.

directions.direction: Modelling and simulation combined with experimental validation to predict optimal heat treatment conditions for phase transformation.
directions.assessment: Using simulation to optimize thermal schedules is promising and informs experimental design. However, while this is complementary and informative, it is more of a tool rather than a single intervention hypothesis in itself.

choice.direction: Tailored post-sintering aging heat treatment to induce fine, ordered TiNi intermetallic precipitates for precipitation strengthening.
choice.why: This direction directly intervenes on the microstructure of a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary HEA to create a dual-phase microstructure with uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates. The mechanism (precipitation strengthening) is well supported by prior evidence (e.g., PMC11396108::web::001::abstract and PMC7513041::web::002::1_introduction) and established physical principles, and it is feasible using available processing techniques like spark plasma sintering followed by aging heat treatment.
